# Copper September 2012 - Copper prices broke out of their prior trading range $100/t either side of $7500/t and moved comfortably above $8000/t following decisive action from central bankers across the globe, while the potential for a boost to demand from a major infrastructure spend in China added fundamental fuel to the price fire sparked by easier money. Copper held on to most of these gains to post its strongest monthly rise since the New Year price rally of January. - A downgrade to our global demand forecast for 2012 has flipped our market balance from deficit to surplus. We now foresee supply exceeding demand by ~100kt in 2012, i.e. a broadly balanced market and full year prices averaging $7997/t. This implies copper cash quotes will average $8100/t in the final quarter in part owing to the stronger market sentiment that has already materialised. - Over the summer increasing evidence has emerged that refined consumption has continued to struggle in the face of tepid economic conditions across the globe. As a result we have cut our forecast of world refined consumption growth in 2012 to 1.9% from 2.7% after we cut our expectations for Europe and China in 2012. Europe consumption has been reduced by 100kt and China by 58kt as our full year predictions were no longer achievable given the current tempo of the market. In this edition we focus our attention on the important Asian markets of Taiwan, China and Japan. While there are some positives to be had it is clear that significant portions of the market are facing adverse economic headwinds that will take some time to overcome. Given the lack of momentum, the recent pick up in prices provides yet another reason for consumers to sit idly on the sidelines and await further developments. - This month has seen a wide range of spot selling terms quoted, but with only a few tenders reported. ## Market Developments 

Copper prices broke out of their prior trading range of $100/t either side of $7500/t and moved comfortably above $8000/t following ‘decisive’ action from central bankers across the globe, while the potential for a boost to demand from a major infrastructure spend in China added fundamental fuel to the price fire, sparked by easier money.  Copper held on to most of these gains to post its strongest monthly rise since the New Year price rally of January. 

**Bank moves central to price action** Prices had already begun to edge upwards at the start of September as traders returned from their summer holidays and in the mood to push the market higher.  Volumes of metal traded and open interest picked up accordingly from the August lull as market participants reopened positions and placed bets on moves from central bankers.  The European Central Bank made the first move with its plan to ease borrowing costs for indebted nations through a bond purchase programme but it was news further east that really set the market alight.  China announced RMB1 trillion Yuan ($150Bn) of infrastructure spending in a bid to support the domestic economy and reinvigorate slowing activity, which resulted in LME cash quotes soaring by 3.5% ($250/t) on the 7<sup>th</sup> of the month.  The sharp rise also drew interest from technical traders after copper broke through its 200 day moving average to add further impetus to price momentum.  Cash quotes subsequently consolidated above the $8000/t level as the focus switched to the US Federal Reserve and whether it would launch another round of quantitative easing.  The Fed failed to disappoint as champagne was broken against the bow of QEIII and prices fizzed some 4% ($300/t) higher on the 14<sup>th</sup> of September. The closing price of $8362/t that day proved to be the high water mark for the month, with the market gradually ebbing lower as traders took profits.  This was despite the Bank of Japan getting in on the action with its own asset purchase programme amid concern over its economy in the face of sluggish export markets. 

**China infrastructure plan to boost economy…** The key fundamental news in the month was of course the announcement of Chinese infrastructure spending, which spurred hopes of an imminent upturn in demand, despite the fact that it will be spread over several years.  Chinese industrial and economic activity has been slowing for most of this year, despite prior spending announcements which have included plans to bring forward infrastructure spending in addition to home appliance purchase incentive schemes.  There have also been cuts to banks’ reserve requirements and the key lending rate.  However, economic activity in general has continued to slow while copper demand has failed to turn decisively higher.  The latest announcement includes 25 urban rail transit projects, in addition to spending on roads, ports and waterways and at least in part reflects the failure of previous

efforts to kick start the economy, with the home appliance scheme proving particularly disappointing for copper especially. **…but too little too late for copper demand** The Chinese infrastructure spending plan is indeed positive for copper, but only at the margin as the latest round of targets are not particularly large consumers of copper. Although cable makers and rod mills are starting to feel some benefit from energy projects, the upturn has proved to be too weak for us to maintain our full year 7% refined demand growth forecast. We remain of the view that there will be a fourth quarter upturn but the performance to date has forced us to tone down its strength and we have clipped 75 percentage points from China to leave our latest growth estimate at 6.25% for 2012. We have, however, upgraded our projection for 2013 as many of the measures announced are likely to have their biggest impact next year. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

**Chinese spot demand hit by higher prices** Shipments of refined metal into China edged lower in August from the prior month, although the sharper contraction in exports resulted in net imports actually gaining on July. Imports totalled 251kt, a 6.6% year-on-year rise, while exports were just 1.7kt to register their third consecutive month-on-month decline. Our analysis reveals that deliveries into bonded warehouses increased only nominally in August, with at least some of the rise in spot shipments that we saw last month having ended up there. We understand that traders shifted material to China in anticipation of improving demand in the final part of the year owing to expectations of rising infrastructure spending. We estimate that bonded warehouse stocks currently stand at around 600kt, a similar level to the end of August. The sharp rise on the LME, which SHFE prices failed to keep pace with, resulted in the arbitrage widening and as a result imported material became less attractive. Moreover, the increase in prices also meant that it was also more expensive to take material out of bonded warehouses because the nominal value of VAT that would need to b

e paid had increased following the run up in prices. It goes without saying that Chinese customers also scaled back purchases in a direct response to higher costs. The resulting softer demand for imported copper kept bonded warehouse stocks at elevated levels and caused premia to dip to $40-$60/t from $50-$75/t last month. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 180 10

**Stocks shortage keeps European premia elevated** In Europe, premia remain elevated although as we noted last month, though this is not because of healthy demand conditions. After longer than expected shutdowns through August, semis producers had been hoping for an upturn in September but orders have failed to receive a meaningful lift. In fact, as a result of weaker than expected demand so far this year we have been forced to lower our expectations of demand in Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2012 Page 3 of 20 Copper Monthly Update 2012 across much of Europe but notably in Germany, cutting ~90kt from our projection. Adjustments elsewhere in Europe have been widespread but less severe with downgrades across much of the region. With demand sluggish, it is the supply side of the equation, in combination with a shortage of stocks, that is underpinning the strength in premia, which remain at around $80-$90/t in North West Europe. In the US, premia also stayed at similar levels to last month, with cathode available for 6-7c/lb. While demand in North America is faring better than in Europe, it could hardly be described as strong with end use consumption continuing to bump along rather than move decisively higher. At least recent data from the housing market points to future growth from this sector. A key reason for high premia ex-China is the lack of available stocks, with material held in exchange warehouses remaining at low levels, while cathode that is there is often stuck at the back of a long queue. LME inventories moved lower from the start of September and touched a new low for the year of 213kt on 18th of the month before large shipments into Busan in South Korea and New Orleans in the US pushed stocks back up. As of 26th September LME warehouses hold 220kt of copper, with only 16kt in Europe and the balance split between Asia and North America. Copper held in COMEX sheds held relatively stable at 46kt, while there was an increase in exchange inventories in China. SHFE stocks rose to 167kt from 158kt at the end of August as rising smelter production (after maintenance shutdowns), a cash to three month backwardation and a general higher price environment drew material onto exchange. **Demand

downgrades flip market into surplus** We have outlined some of the changes to our demand projections above and these have resulted in our global estimate moving lower to 20.1Mt, marking growth of 1.9% this year. The loss of 229kt of demand has been the key factor in the change to our balance, despite disruptions to the supply side continuing apace. The latest production set backs mean that we have used up 4.7% of our 5% allowance already, although it is important to note that increased disruptions do not necessarily alter our market balance on their own. As they occur, we simply use up our generic allowance in tandem with cutting specific mine output. It is only when our 5% allowance is exceeded that we would need to reduce our global production forecast to reflect an interruption at a particular operation. As such, it is weaker demand that has flipped our market balance from deficit to surplus. We now foresee supply exceeding demand by ~100kt in 2012, i.e. a broadly balanced market and full year prices averaging $7997/t. This implies copper cash quotes will average $8100/t in the final quarter in part owing to the stronger market sentiment that has already materialised. In the very short term price action is likely to be muted owing to the holiday in China through the first week of October. Beyond that, and in the absence of meaningful fundamental news, we anticipate that prices will largely be driven by macro news. **Medium term outlook reiterated** Our outlook over the next few years has not significantly altered and we still forecast a meaningful surplus in 2013 and 2014, although because stock days of consumption remain below our long-term average of 65, prices should remain well supported at least into next year. ## Consumption 

Over the summer increasing evidence has emerged that refined consumption has continued to struggle in the face of tepid economic conditions across the globe.  As a result we have cut our forecast of world refined consumption growth in 2012 to 1.9% from 2.7% after we cut our expectations for Europe and China in 2012.  Europe consumption has been reduced by 100kt and China by 58kt as our full year predictions were no longer achievable given the current tempo of the market.  In this edition we focus our attention on the important Asian markets of Taiwan, China and Japan.  While there are some positives to be had it is clear that significant portions of the market are facing adverse economic headwinds that will take some time to overcome.  Given the lack of momentum, the recent pick up in copper prices provides yet another reason for consumers to sit idly on the sidelines and await further market developments. 

### **Taiwan** 

**Taiwanese fabricators endure tough local market conditions** The Taiwanese market continues to struggle through 2012.  Total semis production for the year to July reached 412kt down 9.5% year-on-year on the 455kt manufactured in the same period of 2011.  Output of alloy rods and bars dropped 8.7% to 58kt from 64kt a year ago while production of flat rolled products fell 13.6% to 135kt from 156kt in the same period a year earlier.  Output of the most important semimanufactured product, copper wire rod, also fell declining 7.0% to 218kt in Jan-Jul 2012 compared to 235kt in the prior year.  But here at least the recent trend has been more positive with production in July climbing 7.7% year-on-year to 33kt.  Despite falling output in July of alloy rods and bars (-7.4%) and flat rolled products (-5.2%), the 7.7% increase in copper wire rod output was sufficient to boost total semis output to register a 1.0% year-on-year rise in the month of July. 

**Power cable and wire rod exports are the only strong sectors** The main factor supporting copper wire rod output has been the strength of export demand which rose 12% year-on-year in Jan-Jul 2012.  Mills have limited the decline in their volumes into China/Hong Kong to only 7% but have been able to dramatically increase their shipments to Thailand and the Philippines to serve the expanding auto components business.  Domestic sales of wire rod to the Taiwanese wire and cable industry have dropped by 2% due to a modest decline in total production.  The large volume energy cables sector is the best product line with volumes up 3% year-on-year in the year to July. High and medium voltage power cable demand is healthy but low voltage power cable is weaker.  There has also been some improvement in building wire demand following an increase in housing starts for multi dwelling units.

However other wire and cable product segments are clearly suffering.  Electronic wire output slumped 21%, copper communication cable fell 14% and enamelled wire dropped by 13%. 

### **China** 

**Mixed trend amongst rod mills production plans** Although increased copper power cable orders are starting to be placed with larger wire and cable manufacturers, leading to a noticeable increase in capacity utilisation rates through August and into September, this has yet to be of sufficient scale to influence activity in the rod market.  Mills have announced conflicting production plans for September with some producers raising their targeted output, while others have cut their forecasts, suggesting there is little change in the overall momentum of the market.  The announcement of QE3 has boosted copper market sentiment and prices, but in the short term this represents another impediment to improving volumes in the rod business.  It seems that relatively few consumers were prompted to return to the market for fear that prices would rise further.  Most were content to sit on the sidelines and await copper price developments with no pressing need to buy given ample inventory levels relative to short term requirements.  There is little indication of any real improvement in building wire or winding wire orders and it is probable that copper prices will ease back before attempting another move higher.  Some of the new large rod projects that are commissioning are beginning to contribute tonnage, although the pace of their ramp up is inevitably quite low in the current market environment.  New entrants have chosen to discount their processing fees in a bid to capture some initial market share.  The most positive news has come from Jiangxi Copper who now expect to exceed their annual rod production target of 395kt based on current monthly output of 35-36kt. 

**Semis production continues to increase** Official data reveals a 10.8% rise in total Chinese semis production in the year to August.  The year to date total reached 7,335kt with output in August at 976kt up about 2% on a sequential basis from July.  Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Anhui, Jiangsu and Guangdong remain the dominant provinces for semis production collectively accounting for over 70% of the total.   While production growth has been rapid in the provinces of Anhui (+34%), Jiangxi (+24%) and Zhejiang (+15%) so far this year, output has fallen in Jiangsu (-10%) and Guangdong (-4%). Interestingly, some of the fastest expansion in semis production is now being seen in those provinces where output has traditionally been of smaller scale.  It is now increasing as the semis industry expands its footprint geographically. Neither is this growth exclusively concentrated in Eastern provinces with both Gansu and Qinghai provinces in the West now seeing rapid growth from a very low base.  This suggests that the expansion in Chinese semis production and copper demand will be much broader based in future and also that

### **Japan** **Industry associations downgrade fiscal year outlooks** The two main industry associations reporting on the downstream Japanese copper sector have downgraded their forecasts for the current fiscal year ending March 31st 2013. The Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers Association has lowered its forecast to 695kt versus 680kt in the previous fiscal year which represents a growth rate of only 2.2%. Output in August 2012 reached 56kt, a 3.3% rise from the same month a year ago, and was the fourth successive month to show an increase. The brightest end use market sector was construction which posted a 9.3% year-on-year advance following on from a 14.4% year-on-year surge in July. The trend is encouraging as construction accounts for around 40% of total shipments by volume. Shipments of automotive wiring harnesses also rose by 2.5% year-on-year. This is at a much lesser rate than in previous months as the year-onyear growth rate of automobile production has normalised now that the year-ago effects of the disruption to vehicle assembly have drifted out of the system. However, some weaknesses still remain. Power cable orders from the utilities fell for the 13th successive month in August, although the rate of the decline did moderate to a decline of only 1.7% yearon-year. Exports also remain very depressed due to the strength of the Yen, falling 10.8% year-on-year in August. **Brass mills expectations weakening** The Japan Copper and Brass Association has also revised its views lower for the balance of the fiscal year after the poor first half. It now expects output to decline by 2.2% to 788kt compared to a previous forecast of a 2.4% increase to 825kt. Output has now declined for the 14th consecutive month with August Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2012 Page 6 of 20 Copper Monthly Update production dropping 6.5% from year ago levels to 66kt. One worrying signal is the emerg

ing weakness of the copper strip sector.  This had seen strong sequential monthly gains through the first half of the 2012 calendar year but has slowed recently.  The problem is not automobile connector demand because strip manufacturers report that their operating rates remain very close to maximum.  The cause is softening demand from semiconductor lead frame manufacturers and from the home appliance sector.  Sales of digital devices and home appliances were lower than expected even though the original sales budgets were quite conservative.  Manufacturers had hoped that the second half of this fiscal year would see a recovery in their business.  However, they are now revising their production forecast down in the light of weak orders for October and the backdrop of the slowing Japanese, European and Chinese economies. Exports are the weakest component of Japanese brass mill shipments with volumes down 19% year-on-year. 

### **India** 

**Very slow progress on the consumption front in 2012** Indian copper consumption is growing but only at a very sedate pace this year.  Hindalco’s rod production in the second quarter of this calendar year rose by just 3.2% year-onyear, suggesting the local market is expanding but only at a very meagre single digit growth rate.  S&P recently cut its GDP growth projection for the Indian economy to 5.5% this year, down from a 6.5% previously.  The Wood Mackenzie view is that the economy will growth by 5.8% in 2012.  Economic expansion is being constricted by a combination of high interest rates, steep inflation and high energy prices.  The volatility of the copper price has also caused big problems for consumers for budgeting and working capital requirements.  The automotive business is one of the few sectors which is still performing well.  Vehicle production is set to expand by 9.6% this year, despite high fuel prices, which is supportive to the domestic wiring harness business.  Despite the low growth environment, small scale investments are still being made in the downstream sectors.  One of the better known cablemakers, Finolex Cables, is investing Rs1.6Bn ($36M) to expand its cable production capacity at its plants in Roorkee and Urse to rebalance and boost production of different types of wires and cables.  Also Nash Industries (India) Ltd. is nearing the end of civil construction at its new copper tube plant in Karnataka state, Bangalore.  The project is due to be completed in December 2012. 

### **Western Europe** 

**Structural change to adapt to a weaker market** The European sheet and strip market has seen some long overdue structural change to address overcapacity relative to current and predicted levels of future demand.  Aurubis has announced the redundancy of 177 employees from its Finspang flat rolled products facility in Sweden that it acquired from Luvata when it bought the company’s rolled products division in September 2011.  The Finspang plant makes thin copper strip for automotive heat excha

nger applications and its output is marketed worldwide. However, this market segment has been under pressure from substitution losses to aluminium ever since the copper price escalated sharply in 2004/05. Production and equipment will be consolidated into Aurubis’s plants in Zutphen, Netherlands and Buffalo, USA that it also acquired from Luvata. Meanwhile in Italy, Eredi Gnutti, the Italian brass rod and copper sheet and strip manufacturer has acquired Dalmet, a small specialist Italian copper and copper alloy sheet and strip maker with a capacity of 3kta. This is the group’s second acquisition in this sector as it had acquired another northern Italian sheet and strip manufacturer Ilnor in September 2010. The acquisitions were aimed at diversifying the company’s sales away from low value added roofing strip in the domestic market to higher added value copper and alloy products for electrical and electronic uses in export markets within Europe. In Spain, copper wire production has held up close to last year’s levels through the summer. With domestic consumption weakening, production has only been sustained by expanding exports into France, Morocco and Tunisia. utlook for refined metal. After accounting for VAT the arbitrage during the first week of September averaged $116/t (SHFE under LME), but once LME prices started to rally from the 7th September, leaving SHFE in its wake, the arbitrage flared out to highs of almost $700/t at one point. The higher LME copper prices also encouraged merchants to release some scrap into the market allowing smelters (in both Japan and China) to use more of this material which helped producers contain costs and support profits. China’s CSPT raised its minimum TC/RC buying objective to $65/t & 6.5c/lb, although there was no real evidence of business having been conducted at this level. That said a recent deal in India broke through the $60/t & 6c/lb mark. Concentrate supply continued to fall short of expectations and we have marked down mine production further, especially in Chile. Elsewhere, problems at Ok Tedi have also resurfaced, while Rio Tinto announced that production at Oyu Tolgoi will only start in 2013 once power supply agreements have been concluded. TCRC negotiations are likely to be challenging again this year reflecting the ongoing issue of mine production disruptions as well as potential scrap availability. #### **Concentrate market TC/RCs** ||**J**

ntrate||||||||| |_Source: Wood Mackenzie_|||||||||| **Wide range of spot terms as smelters undergo maintenance** This month there has been a wide range of spot selling terms quoted but with only a few tenders reported. As we went to press last month Ivanhoe (Osborne) Pty Ltd. offered 21k wmt of concentrates from its Osborne mine in Queensland, Australia with the tonnage split equally for shipment in October and December of this year. We understand that this material fetched terms in the low 40s and 4s. It is not clear if these headline numbers include any variations to other terms given the low level in comparison to the deals that have been concluded in the recent past. That said Osborne concentrates are ultra clean and can be used for blending and, therefore, could command premium terms as a result. In the meantime, Sterlite is rumoured to have bought a menu of two concentrate qualities, including Chilean material grading <0.4% As (at seller’s option) at terms of $61/t and 6.1c/lb. Meanwhile we understand that a parcel from Northparkes was sold in the mid-50s and 5s for prompt shipment

. Goldfields La Cima was also in the market with Cerro Corona concentrates, but due to back pricing options it is difficult to know how the buyer would have valued the QP optionality when translating the deal into plain vanilla TC/RCs.  This parcel is likely to be used locally for blending. 

It has been reported that following a scheduled maintenance that lasted for around 50 days, the Chuquicamata smelter is back in production.  At the start of the year original plans were for an 83 day shut down, however, problems at the flash smelter in Q1 2012 led to an unscheduled maintenance closure of around 45-50 days.  As a result we understand that this latest planned maintenance downtime, which started at the end of July and ended in early September was for a much shorter period.  Upgrades to the flash furnace have been completed (the intention being to shut down the Teniente converters to meet new environmental regulations in 2014) and the operation was restarted on 10th September.  As a result, Codelco appears to have offloaded considerable tonnages of Chuqui concentrates into the market and some estimates suggest that around 150kt have been sold thus far in 2012. 

**Issues resurface at Ok Tedi and add to total disruptions** We understand that there was a recent concentrate pipeline blockage that lasted for 7 days at Ok Tedi.  Although this problem has been resolved, there are also rumours of an issue with the in-pit crusher which may see the unit out of commission for 2 weeks. 

So far this year, disruptions at the mine account for just shy of 5% of our initial mine production forecast for 2012.  These have been the result of lower than forecast head grades and on-going operational issues at some major producers.  As yet, production has not been interrupted by industrial action to the same extent as during 2011, although several labour contracts are due for renegotiation at some large producers including Antamina, Andina, Anglo American Sur and Southern Copper before the end of the year. 

**2013 Mating season fast approaching** It appears that once again, ahead of LME week and the influx of market participants into London, spot treatment and refining charges are trending higher and, as might be expected, there is a growing differential between spot buying and selling terms.  It should come as little surprise that China’s CSPT has

raised its minimum spot buying TC/RC objective to similar levels to last year’s long-term benchmark TC/RCs ($63.5/t & 6.35c/lb).  Historically, when there has been a large differential between prevailing spot terms and the prior year’s benchmark TC/RCs, this has provided at the very least a psychological advantage to either the buyer or the seller when entering Mating Season discussions.  That said spot rates could rise further in Q4 with additional smelter maintenance closures upcoming in Q4.  For the 2013 negotiations, t

he impact of spot terms will be broadly neutral and the main focus of the early discussions will be on the likely net additions to concentrate supplies and primary smelter capacity.  In this context, notable new mine projects and restarts contributing to next year’s concentrate supplies include Antapaccay (Peru), Bisha (Eritrea), Caserones (Chile), Codelco MMH (Chile), Oyu Tolgoi (Mongolia), Pinto Valley (USA), Tayahua (Mexico) and possibly Frontier (DRC).  We would also expect higher output at Collahuasi, Escondida, Grasberg, Los Bronces, Lumwana and Salobo.  According to our estimates, the net increase in copper in concentrate production in 2013 relative to this year will be almost 1.9Mt.  Note that this figure takes no account of disruptions which, when catered for, reduces the uplift to 1.1Mt.  As might be expected, China will contribute the lion’s share of additional primary smelting capacity (Dongying, Huixing, Jinchuan Guangdong, Tongling, Zhongtiaoshan, Zijin etc.), accounting for 87% of the 670kt increase.   Average primary smelter operating rates have fallen from 83% in 2011 to an expected 81.3% this year. Taking into account the net additions to mines and smelters, we would expect primary smelter capacity utilisation rates to average 84.5% next year.  Note that this is likely to be the maximum rate achievable, as it requires concentrate stocks to remain at a similar low level to this year (28 days of consumption).  The 50kt copper in concentrate ‘surplus’ shown in our balances should not be interpreted as the market moving into surplus.  This is merely an uplift in pipeline stocks that is required to maintain a minimum level of inventories (i.e. 28 days) in a growing market.  And while rising utilisation rates will be welcome news for custom smelters, it should be borne in mind that the optimal rate for the industry is higher than this at 88%.  Taking all of these factors into account, it would seem that once again the industry will be faced with another year of difficult negotiations especially as we believe that the pace of scrap that will come to the market will be lower again in 2013 as it has been so far this year. 

**Chinese concentrate imports rise** Copper concentrate imports into China in August maintained their upward trend, rising to 695kt, a 23% increase on July levels but up by just 3% on year ago levels.  So far in 2012, concentrate imports have increased by a hefty 14% compared to the same period last year, to total 4.644Mt.  Chinese smelter profits remain squeezed as the differential between SHFE and LME prices has widened again over the latter part of September.  That said we understand that some smelters have raised their utilisation rates in anticipation of an uptick in demand following the end of the low season for demand.  This may also reflect the return of some smelters to production following maintenance closures.  Reports suggest that there were maintenance shutdowns at Chifeng Jinjian, Chifeng Yunnan Copper a

nd Yantai during August.  As we noted last month, several smelters will undertake maintenance through Q4. These include Guixi, Dongying, the Ausmelt furnace at Daye and possibly Jinchuan in December. 

**Further delay for Jabal Sayid** Initial production of copper concentrates from Barrick Gold’s Jabal Sayid mine in Saudi Arabia is now reported to be delayed until 2014.  This is due to the fact that the mine’s safety and security standards need to be brought into line with Saudi regulations related to the use of explosives.  The project, which is rated to produce 55kt/a of copper in concentrate was originally forecast to commence exports during the second half of 2012. 

**Tritton off-take agreement** Australian miner, Straits Resources announced a life of mine off-take agreement with Glencore for production from its Tritton Copper mine in New South Wales  The deal was part of a package of measures which included Glencore providing a short-term A$20M finance facility to Straits and underwriting up to A$40M of an ‘entitlement offer’ to existing shareholders.  The Tritton mine produces ~30kt/a of copper in concentrate. 

**Canadian smelter environmental upgrade** The $2Bn Clean AER (atmospheric emissions reduction) project at Vale’s Copper Cliff smelter in Ontario reached an important milestone this month with the delivery of the first of four new convertors.  The project which is due to be completed by 2015 is intended to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions by 70% as well as a reduction in dust and metals emissions of around 40%.  The smelter complex treats copper/nickel concentrates produced at Vale’s Clarabelle mill sourced from its own mines as well as others in the Sudbury area. 

**Pan Pacific upstream investment** Japanese smelting company, Pan Pacific Copper (PPC) acquired a 40% share in the Vicuna Joint Exploration Agreement (JEA) from Japanese government organisation, JOGMEC.  The JEA covers a large land package in Chile and Argentina that includes the advanced exploration stage Los Helados Project in Chile and the Filo del Sol Project in Argentina.  PPC which is jointly owned by JX Nippon Mining and Metals Corp (66%) and Mitsui Mining and Smelting (34%) is currently constructing the Caserones copper and molybdenum, project, which is located around 10km from Los Helados.  The remaining 60% stake in the Vicuna JEA is retained by Canadian explorer NGex Resources. 

**Indonesian export ban may be delayed** Reports from Indonesia suggest that a proposed ban on concentrate exports, due to be implemented in 2014 may be delayed to allow companies more time to invest in sufficient smelting and refining capacity to process all of the country’s mine production domestically.  With Gresik, Indonesia’s only existing copper smelter, capable of processing around 1.1Mt/a of concentrate, exports from the country are forecast to be ~1.0Mt in 2012.  The amount of concentrate available for export is forecast to rise to ~2.5M dmt by 2015 as output picks up at th

e country’s two producers, PT Freeport Indonesia’s Grasberg mine and Newmont’s Batu Hijau operation. Norilsk Nickel is reported to have signed a letter of intent with Indonesia’s Ministry of Trade and Industry to build a copper smelting and refining complex in Indonesia in conjunction with local company, PT Nusantara. The project could produce 200-400kt/a of refined metal. ## Production news 

**Glencore first half production level** While Glencore’s proposed merger with Xstrata dominated the headlines, first half copper production from mines controlled by the Swiss-based company was unchanged from the equivalent period in 2011 at 170kt.  Ongoing commissioning of the Mutanda operation (60% Glencore) in DRC saw production rise from 26kt in the first six months of 2011 to 38kt in 2012.

This increase was balanced by lower production elsewhere, particularly at Mopani Copper Mines in Zambia (73.1% Glencore) where planned maintenance of the Mufulira smelter saw first half refined production from the company’s own mines down by 21% on 2011 at 39kt.  Despite increased mining rates at the Katanga Mining operations in the DRC (75.2% owned by Glencore) plant throughput was adversely impacted by interruptions to power supplies and first half production remained constant at 43kt. 

**Antofagasta output rises** The continued ramp up of operations at the Esperanza mine in northern Chile saw Antofagasta’s first half production reach 336kt, a 16% increase over the equivalent period in 2011.  Despite lower than anticipated mill throughput, payable copper in concentrate at Esperanza was 68.2kt during the first half of 2012, a 133% uplift on the same period during 2011.  First half production at Los Pelambres was 197kt of paid copper in concentrate, up by 2% on 2011 while processing of higher grade ore from the Mirador pit saw first half production at El Tesoro rise by 17% to 53kt.  During September, Antofagasta announced that SNC-Lavalin has been awarded a contract to provide overall management, detailed engineering, procurement and construction management (EPCM) services for the Antucoya project.  Antucoya, which is forecast to produce 80kt/a of SxEw cathode is located close to the company’s existing Michilla mine in northern Chile. 

**Mount Margaret production** Xstrata announced the start of ore production at its Mount Margaret operation in northwest Queensland.  Ore from Mount Margaret will be trucked to the Ernest Henry concentrator for processing.  The Mount Margaret project was acquired from Exco Resources in 2011 and comprises two deposits; E1 and Monakoff which are located 8km and 21km respectively from Ernest Henry.  The project is forecast to contribute 30kt/a to Ernest Henry’s overall production for 5 years. 

**Phu Kham upgrade** PanAust Limited announced the commissioning of a mill expansion at its Phu Kham mine in Laos. The $95M project is intended to increase ore processing capacity from 12Mt/a to 16Mt/a and improve flotation recovery to compensate for forecast lower head grades in coming years.  The mine is forecast to produce between 65kt and 70kt of copper in concentrate during 2013, marginally higher than 2012 output. 

**Palabora repair complete** Palabora Mining has reported that ore hoisting resumed at its South African mine on September 9<sup>th</sup> .  Failure of a guide rope in early July had resulted in damage to the skip loading station in the mine’s production shaft. 

**Copper Mountain mill repairs** Canadian producer Copper Mountain Mining announced that a planned maintenance shutdown to implement repairs intended to improve mill utilisation at its mine in British Columbia had been successfully completed.  With plant throughput now expected to achieve the design rate of 35kt/d, total copper production for the ye

ar is now forecast to be approximately 30kt of copper in concentrate. 

**Philippines mine closure** Philex Mining Corp has closed its Padcal operation for an indefinite period as it seeks to contain leaks from the mine’s tailings pond.  The mine was previously forecast to produce ~20kt of copper in concentrate this year with the bulk of its output destined for Pan Pacific’s Saganoseki smelter in Japan. 

**New mining regulations in Philippines** The Philippines government announced new rules banning mining in locations designated as ‘agriculture’ or ‘tourism’ areas and imposed tighter environmental standards and increased royalties for the rest of the industry.  It remains uncertain how the new regulations will (further) impact the Tampakan project on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao which is being developed by a joint venture between Xstrata and Indophil Resources.  Progress on the project, rated to produce 450kt/a of copper in concentrate, has been stalled because the proposed site partly lies in the province of South Cotabato where open pit mining is prohibited despite national regulations that allow it.  The new regulations state that conflicts between local and national regulations would be resolved through the Department of the Interior and Local Government.  Other potential copper mining developments in the Philippines that could potentially be impacted by the new rules include St Augustine Gold & Copper’s King-king project, Copper Development Corporation’s Hinoba-an project and the potential restart of the Batong Buhay copper and gold mine.

ing of the concentrator at its Degrussa project in Western Australia is underway with design throughput of 4kt/d targeted for early 2013.
